questiontext.text: <p>Which three primary categories constitute the foundation of a comprehensive scholarly commentary on a historical text?</p>

answer.text: <p>Philological (linguistic/grammatical), historical/cultural (realia/context), and intertextual (citations/allusions/text reuse).</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Standard critical commentaries address linguistic difficulty, historical realia, and intertextual relationships with other literary works.</p>

answer.text: <p>Financial, legal, marketing, and advertising.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. These are corporate commercial business categories, not humanities scholarly commentary domains.</p>

answer.text: <p>HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and PHP.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. These are web development programming languages.</p>

answer.text: <p>Hardcover, paperback, audiobook, and ebook.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. These are commercial book publishing formats.</p>

name.text: 02 Question: Inline vs Stand-Off Commentary Architecture

questiontext.text: <p>Why do modern digital critical editions strongly prefer 'stand-off' commentary notes over 'inline' `<note>` elements?</p>

answer.text: <p>Stand-off notes reside outside the primary narrative body (e.g. in `<back>`), preventing editorial prose from interrupting the syntactic flow of the source text and facilitating multiple overlapping commentary layers.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Stand-off markup maintains clean separation between source text and editorial interpretation, allowing multiple scholars to annotate the same coordinates without tag overlapping collisions.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because inline notes are illegal under Canadian intellectual property laws.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Markup architecture is an engineering and philological decision, not a legal statute.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because web browsers refuse to display any webpage containing inline notes.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Browsers can render any valid HTML/XML structure.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because stand-off notes automatically delete the source text to save server bandwidth.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Stand-off notes point to the source text via URI targets; they never delete it.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>In TEI P5, how can an editor attach a commentary note to an arbitrary sequence of words that crosses paragraph or line boundaries without violating XML nesting?</p>

answer.text: <p>By placing empty `<anchor xml:id="...">` milestone elements at the start and end of the passage and referencing both IDs in the note's `@target` attribute.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Empty anchor milestones provide precise coordinate points in the text tree without creating illegal overlapping XML hierarchies.</p>

answer.text: <p>By deleting the closing `</p>` tags so that elements can overlap freely.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Deleting closing tags produces malformed XML that immediately crashes parsers.</p>

answer.text: <p>By converting the whole paragraph into an uncompressed JPEG picture.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Converting text to raster images destroys machine readability and searchability.</p>

answer.text: <p>By renaming all tags `<div1>`, `<div2>`, and `<div3>`.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Arbitrary tag renaming does not resolve structural overlapping.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>How does the Tesserae intertextual discovery tool identify literary text reuse across classical texts?</p>

answer.text: <p>It uses frequency-weighted n-gram matching, calculating scores based on the rarity of shared words and their proximity within sentences.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Tesserae finds intertextual allusions by scoring pairs of shared words inversely proportional to their overall corpus frequencies and positional distance.</p>

answer.text: <p>It reads the author's personal diary to find written confessions of plagiarism.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Tesserae is an automated computational text analysis tool operating on digital corpora.</p>

answer.text: <p>It translates both texts into binary Morse code and compares the audio frequencies.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Tesserae evaluates lexical frequency vectors, not acoustic sound waves.</p>

answer.text: <p>It checks whether both authors purchased books from the same bookstore.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Ancient authors lived centuries before modern commercial book chains.</p>

name.text: 05 Question: W3C Web Annotation Data Model

questiontext.text: <p>In the W3C Web Annotation Data Model (JSON-LD), what are the two essential components linked together by an `Annotation` object?</p>

answer.text: <p>The `body` (the commentary content, translation, or tag) and the `target` (the specific digital resource or text fragment being annotated).</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. W3C Web Annotation formally links a Target (what is being annotated) to a Body (the commentary or analytical content) via a declared Motivation.</p>

answer.text: <p>The `username` and the `password`.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. These are authentication credentials, not W3C annotation components.</p>

answer.text: <p>The `printer` and the `paper`.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. These are physical printing hardware elements.</p>

answer.text: <p>The `input` and the `output`.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. These are general software engineering concepts.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>How does a W3C `TextQuoteSelector` anchor an annotation to a specific phrase in a web document even if the underlying HTML shifts slightly?</p>

answer.text: <p>By recording an `exact` matching string along with a `prefix` context and a `suffix` context to locate the unique occurrence robustly.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. A TextQuoteSelector uses exact text plus surrounding prefix and suffix context, ensuring stable anchoring even across dynamic DOM updates.</p>

answer.text: <p>By calculating the physical weight of the reader's laptop computer.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Hardware weight is completely irrelevant to digital text selectors.</p>

answer.text: <p>By permanently locking the webpage so that nobody can ever edit it again.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. TextQuoteSelectors are designed specifically to handle documents that undergo minor edits.</p>

answer.text: <p>By converting all surrounding words into secret passwords.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Selectors operate on transparent plaintext context strings.</p>

name.text: 07 Question: Linking Notes to Linked Open Data Authorities

questiontext.text: <p>Why is enriching commentary notes with Linked Open Data URIs (such as Pleiades for places and VIAF for people) methodologically valuable?</p>

answer.text: <p>It disambiguates entities unambiguously and links the edition to the global semantic web, enabling automated cross-project querying and interactive spatial mapping.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Resolvable authority URIs eliminate naming ambiguities (e.g. distinguishing Antioch in Syria from Antioch in Pisidia) and integrate the text with global knowledge graphs.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because it increases the purchase price of the digital edition on commercial ebook stores.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Linked Open Data promotes open scholarship, not commercial price gouging.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because university servers crash if an XML file contains fewer than ten web links.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Servers do not require external links to function.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because it allows the user to play 3D computer games inside the footnote.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Linked Data facilitates rigorous scholarly research, not video gaming.</p>

name.text: 08 Question: AI Hallucinations in Historical Commentary

questiontext.text: <p>When using generative AI to assist in drafting historical commentary notes, what is a frequent, treacherous hallucination hazard?</p>

answer.text: <p>Fabricating scholarly citations (inventing non-existent books, authors, or journal page numbers) and projecting anachronistic modern theological or social concepts onto premodern sources.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. LLMs frequently generate completely fabricated but highly convincing bibliographies and project anachronistic concepts back into antiquity.</p>

answer.text: <p>Translating the text into completely flawless ancient Sumerian cuneiform.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Models typically fail at low-resource ancient scripts rather than producing flawless translations.</p>

answer.text: <p>Refusing to write any sentence that contains the letter 'e'.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Models have no constraint against standard letters unless explicitly prompted.</p>

answer.text: <p>Deleting all comments made by the instructor on Moodle.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Generating text in a chat prompt cannot interact with or delete remote Moodle forum posts.</p>

name.text: 09 Question: Distinguishing Literary Allusion from Coincidental Overlap

questiontext.text: <p>Why must algorithmic text-reuse matches (e.g. from Tesserae) be verified by a human scholar before being published as an intertextual commentary note?</p>

answer.text: <p>Because statistical algorithms frequently flag coincidental collocations of common grammatical words or stock idioms that lack any intentional literary or historical allusion.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Algorithms detect string similarities; only human philologists can evaluate whether shared vocabulary reflects genuine intertextual dialogue, formulaic convention, or random chance.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because computers are legally prohibited from publishing literary criticism.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Computational analysis is widely published in academic venues.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because all ancient authors wrote completely unique sentences that never shared a single word.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Historical texts share vast lexical conventions and literary allusions.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because digital editions are only allowed to have one commentary note per chapter.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Digital editions impose no arbitrary limits on commentary density.</p>

name.text: 10 Question: Quality Assurance for TEI Commentary Markup

questiontext.text: <p>What is the critical validation requirement for stand-off commentary notes before compiling a digital edition?</p>

answer.text: <p>Verifying that every `@target` URI correctly resolves to an existing `xml:id` in the text body, and that all cited authorities resolve to valid HTTP URIs.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Dangling pointers and dead links undermine the reliability of a digital edition; every anchor target must resolve cleanly during validation.</p>

answer.text: <p>Ensuring that every note is written in iambic pentameter verse.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Scholarly commentary is written in analytical academic prose.</p>

answer.text: <p>Confirming that every single word in the text has at least three footnotes.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Commentary should be judicious, focused on genuine cruxes, rather than cluttering clear text.</p>

answer.text: <p>Deleting all original manuscript text so only the commentary remains.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. A critical commentary accompanies and elucidates the primary source, rather than erasing it.</p>
